claims.text: The damaged component is a nickel-based superalloy turbine blade.
Traditional fusion welding is ineffective for this component because it presents a high risk of hot cracking.
The proposed intervention is cold-spray deposition using pre-alloyed powder whose composition matches the substrate.
The cold-sprayed repair will receive a post-deposition stress-relief heat treatment below the substrate melting point.
Cold spray is a solid-state process in which high-velocity particles deform mechanically and bond to the substrate without melting.
Avoiding melting also avoids the fusion-welding thermal cycles that can induce hot cracking.
Solid-state cold-spray deposition will preserve desirable microstructural characteristics of the nickel-based superalloy.
The repair will produce a thin deposit.
The repair deposit will be dense.
The repair deposit will be nearly fully metallurgically bonded to the base material.
The repair deposit will exhibit a refined grain structure.
The repaired zone will have mechanical properties approximating those of the original material.
Cold-spray repair will markedly reduce hot cracking relative to fusion-welding repair.
Cold-spray repair will perform better than fusion-welded repair under high-temperature and cyclic-loading conditions.
Full melting and solidification during fusion welding cause significant hot-cracking risk.
Fusion-welded repairs have inferior mechanical properties under aggressive operating conditions.
Interfacial bonding and deposit densification may limit long-term mechanical performance under operational stresses.
